title: WAL, checkpoints, crash recovery and replication
one_liner: PostgreSQL logs every change to a sequential journal (WAL) before touching data files, so it can recover from crashes and feed replicas.
analogy: WAL is a ship's logbook. You write what you will do first. If the ship sinks, read the log and redo it. Copies of the log go to sister ships.
big_picture: WAL means write-ahead log: a change is logged to disk before the data page is written.
Logging is fast because it is sequential appends. Data pages can be written lazily later.
Every WAL record has an LSN: a byte position in the log that only grows.
A checkpoint flushes dirty pages and notes a safe starting point for recovery.
After a crash, the startup process replays WAL from the last checkpoint (redo).
Replicas get the same WAL stream and replay it. Logical decoding turns WAL into row changes.

flow.detail: A table or index routine registers data and buffers, then calls XLogInsert with a resource manager id.
Header, block references and optional full page images are packed together. A full page image is added if the page was not logged since the last checkpoint.
The backend claims a byte range in the WAL buffers, which gives the record its LSN, then copies the bytes in.
RecordTransactionCommit calls XLogFlush so the log is durable. With synchronous_commit off, the WAL writer flushes later. A dirty page is flushed only after WAL up to its page LSN is on disk.
The checkpointer writes dirty buffers, writes a checkpoint record and updates pg_control with its location.
The startup process reads pg_control, finds the redo point, then reads records one by one and calls each rmgr redo function.
The walsender sends WAL bytes. The walreceiver writes and flushes them. The startup process replays them.
Each record goes to its rmgr decode function. Changes are grouped per transaction and sent to a subscriber.

diagram.claim: A change flows from a backend into WAL, then to disk, replicas and recovery.

interview.q: What is WAL and why does Postgres have it?
answer: WAL is an append-only log of every change.
Rule: log the change first, write the data page later.
Appending is fast and sequential, so commit is cheap.
After a crash, WAL lets Postgres redo lost page changes.
interview.trap: WAL is not a backup or an audit log. It is mainly for crash safety and replication.

answer: LSN is a position in the WAL byte stream.
It is a 64-bit number, type XLogRecPtr in xlogdefs.h.
It only grows. Each page stores the LSN of its last change.
interview.trap: An LSN is not a transaction id. It is a byte offset in the log.

answer: The commit record is inserted into WAL.
XLogFlush forces WAL up to that LSN to disk.
Data pages are not forced to disk at commit.
interview.trap: Commit does not write the table data files. Only WAL must be on disk.

answer: Each kind of change (heap, btree, xact) has an rmgr.
rmgrlist.h lists them with redo, desc and decode functions.
Every record has xl_rmid saying who owns it.
Recovery calls the owner's rm_redo to replay it.
interview.trap: Rmgrs are not processes. They are tables of callbacks.

interview.q: What is a full page write and why is it needed?
answer: Disk may write only part of an 8K page in a crash (torn page).
So the first change to a page after a checkpoint logs the whole page.
Redo restores the page image, then applies later changes.
It is controlled by the full_page_writes setting.
interview.trap: It does not log every change as a full page. Only the first touch after a checkpoint.

answer: It flushes all dirty shared buffers to disk (CheckPointBuffers).
It writes a checkpoint record and stores its location in pg_control.
Recovery can then start from the redo point, not the log start.
Old WAL segments before that point can be removed or recycled.
interview.trap: A checkpoint does not stop the database. It is spread out over time.

answer: The startup process reads pg_control to find the checkpoint.
PerformWalRecovery loops: read record, ApplyWalRecord.
ApplyWalRecord calls the rmgr redo function.
Redo skips a page if its LSN is newer (XLogReadBufferForRedo returns BLK_DONE).
At the end, the startup process writes an end-of-recovery record or checkpoint and the server opens for writes.
interview.trap: Recovery does not undo uncommitted work. Aborted rows are just invisible via MVCC.

interview.q: How does streaming replication move data?
answer: The standby walreceiver connects and asks the walsender for WAL.
The walsender runs XLogSendPhysical and sends WAL bytes.
The walreceiver writes and flushes it, then the startup process replays it.
Synchronous mode makes commit wait in SyncRepWaitForLSN.
interview.trap: Streaming sends WAL bytes, not SQL statements.

interview.q: How is logical decoding different from physical replication?
answer: Physical copies raw WAL, so the replica is a byte-level clone.
Logical decodes WAL into row changes through each rmgr's rm_decode.
LogicalDecodingProcessRecord drives it. ReorderBuffer groups changes per transaction.
Needs wal_level logical and a replication slot.
interview.trap: Logical decoding does not read tables. It reads WAL.

interview.q: If you add a new WAL-logged operation, what must you write?
answer: A record layout and an XLogInsert call with XLogRegisterData or buffers.
A redo function in the rmgr that replays it exactly.
A desc and identify entry so pg_waldump can print it.
Handle decode if logical replication needs it, and add tests.
interview.trap: Forgetting the redo side. Logging without a matching redo breaks recovery and standbys.

contributor_tips: Read src/backend/access/transam/README first. It explains the rules in plain words.
Use src/bin/pg_waldump/pg_waldump.c to see real WAL records while you experiment.
Be careful: redo must be deterministic and must never fail in a critical section.
Start with small things: docs, rmgr desc output, or tests under src/test/recovery.

glossary.meaning: Write-ahead log: sequential journal of all changes.
Log sequence number: a byte position in WAL.
Point where dirty pages are flushed and a recovery start is recorded.
Replaying WAL records to rebuild page changes.
Whole 8K page stored in WAL to guard against torn pages.
Resource manager: callbacks that own one kind of WAL record.

more: wal_level: minimal, replica and logical each log different amounts.
WAL lives in pg_wal as 16MB segment files that are recycled.
Replication slots hold back WAL until a consumer has read it.
Archiving and point-in-time recovery use archive_command and restore_command.
A failure inside a critical section is a PANIC. That is why redo must not fail.
